narration: There's a hole in Antarctica. Two feet wide. It drops through six hundred metres of ice into water no light has ever touched.
visual: Narrow dark borehole in a vast empty ice plain, snow streaming across surface
transition: HARD CUT out. Match the dark circle to shot 02.

narration: In 2020, scientists lowered a robot down that hole. They wanted to measure melting. They found out they'd been measuring the wrong thing.
visual: Yellow robot on a cable descending into the ice shaft

narration: The glacier is called Thwaites. Researchers have another name for it. They call it the Doomsday Glacier. That is not marketing.
visual: Satellite Antarctica, zoom to west coast, pin drop, TITLE CARD
transition: Dip to black 8 frames after title

narration: Antarctica is not land with snow on top. It is rock, buried under an ice sheet up to four kilometres thick.
visual: Cross-section: bedrock, thick ice sheet above, ocean to one side

narration: Stand on that surface, and the real ground sits further below you than a passenger jet flies above you.
visual: Vertical scale: figure on ice, bedrock far below, jet far above

narration: Thwaites itself is roughly the size of Great Britain. One glacier. Larger than most countries on Earth. And it is moving.
visual: Thwaites outline on satellite base, Great Britain silhouette overlaid to scale
camera: Slow zoom out to reveal scale

narration: Here is what makes it dangerous. The rock beneath Thwaites sits below sea level, and it slopes downward as you travel inland.
visual: Side cross-section: bedrock sloping down left-to-right, ice above, water right
camera: Slow lateral truck, left to right
transition: Hard cut. KEEP THIS PLATE - reused in 08, 24, 25.

narration: That means the ocean can reach underneath it. Warm water slides in from the sea and eats the glacier from below.
visual: Shot 07 plate + warm current arrows pushing under the ice base

narration: From above, nothing looks wrong. The surface is white, solid, still. For decades, that surface was all we could actually see.
visual: Aerial drift over featureless white ice plain
transition: Dip to black - end of Act 1

narration: So a British and American team flew onto the ice with a hot water drill, and started melting a hole straight down.
visual: Remote polar field camp: drill rig, hoses, crates, tents. No people

narration: It took days. The borehole had to be kept warm the whole time, or it would freeze shut and swallow the equipment.
visual: Insulated hose descending into a hole in ice, faint steam rising

narration: The robot is called Icefin. Three and a half metres long, thin enough to fit down a shaft barely wider than a dinner plate.
visual: Yellow cylindrical robot in profile, dark background, engineering presentation
transition: Hard cut. KEEP THIS PLATE - reused in 13.

narration: It carries cameras, sonar, and sensors for temperature and salt. A cable feeds power down, and sends data back up.
visual: Shot 12 plate + animated component callout lines and labels

narration: Icefin reached the bottom, swam sideways into the cavity, and became the first machine to see where Thwaites meets the sea.
visual: Robot emerges from ice shaft into vast dark water, lamps switch on

narration: And the ceiling above it was not flat. Not smooth. Not anything the models had drawn. It was carved into shapes.
visual: Underside of glacier from dark water, one hard lamp raking across carved ice
transition: Hard cut - no transition, let the reveal land

narration: Terraces, like a staircase. Deep vertical cracks. Sloped walls. An entire hidden landscape, hanging upside down above the water.
visual: Terraced ice ceiling, deep fissures, sloped walls, lit from below
camera: Tilt up + slow track along ceiling
transition: Hard cut. HERO SHOT - also your thumbnail frame.

narration: Then the team compared melt rates across that landscape, and the result did not match the predictions. Not even close.
visual: Split screen: flat ice plate vs crevassed plate, melt arrows on both

narration: Across the flat stretches, the ice was melting more slowly than expected. Slower. That was better news than anyone had hoped for.
visual: Flat-ice panel alone, slow melt arrows, downward trend line

narration: But inside the cracks, and along the sloped walls, the melting was fast. In places, several times faster than the flat ice.
visual: Crevasse panel alone, rapid melt arrows cutting into walls
camera: Slow push-in, faster arrow animation than 18
transition: Hard cut - the speed contrast IS the point

narration: So the glacier was not dissolving evenly, like an ice cube in a glass. It was being unpicked, along its weak points.
visual: Two ice blocks: left smooth and rounded, right split along sharp seams
transition: Dip to black - end of Act 3

narration: That distinction matters far more than the raw numbers. Here is exactly why it changes every forecast we had.
visual: Kinetic type over darkened, slowly drifting shot-16 plate

narration: Ice that melts evenly shrinks. Slowly. Predictably. You can model that, and project a century ahead with some confidence.
visual: Smooth shrinking volume with a steady confident projection curve

narration: Ice that fails along its cracks does not shrink. It fractures. And fracturing holds, and holds, and then goes all at once.
visual: Real glacier calving - ice face collapsing into water

narration: Now add the ground. The bedrock slopes inland and downward, so every retreat carries the glacier into deeper water.
visual: Shot 07 plate + grounding line retreating down the reverse slope

narration: Deeper water means more warm ocean touching more ice, which pushes the grip point back further, into deeper water again.
visual: IDENTICAL to 24, one step further back
transition: Hard cut. The repeat is the argument.

narration: That is a feedback loop. A system that, once it truly starts, helps itself along without needing any more push.
visual: Circular loop diagram: retreat > warm water > retreat

narration: And I want to be straight with you, because this part gets exaggerated constantly. We do not know Thwaites has crossed that line.
visual: Two-column type: 'What we know' / 'What we don't'

narration: Scientists genuinely disagree on how close it is. Some models say centuries. Anyone giving you a firm date is selling something.
visual: Divergent projection curves fanning into a wide uncertainty cone

narration: Thwaites alone holds enough ice to raise global sea level by half a metre. It also acts as a cork, holding back far more.
visual: Thwaites highlighted, then wider West Antarctic sheet lights up behind

narration: We built a robot to discover our own planet wasn't shaped the way we thought. What would you send a camera into? Subscribe.
visual: Looking up a narrow ice shaft at a distant circle of daylight, lamps receding
